news.2026-10-25-georgie-proces-interdire: In Georgia, the ruling party asks the courts to ban five opposition parties
Georgia’s Constitutional Court held three days of hearings in Batumi on a request to ban the five main opposition parties. It has until June 2027 to rule, with no appeal possible.

From 21 to 23 October, the Constitutional Court examined in Batumi the request of 88 lawmakers from the ruling Georgian Dream party, who want five opposition groups banned: the United National Movement, Coalition for Change, Strong Georgia–Lelo, the Federalists and Gakharia for Georgia [1][2].

The lawmakers accuse these parties of violating Article 23 of the Constitution, which bans parties that seek to overthrow or forcibly change the constitutional order; four parties are defending themselves in court, a fifth is boycotting the proceedings [2].

The court, which has only 7 of its 9 judges in office, must rule by June 2027; its decision will be final, with no appeal in Georgia [2]. The opposition calls it a ploy to remove its main rivals before the next elections [1][2].
Key point: if the court sides with the government, Georgia, a candidate for European Union membership, would be left without its main opposition parties [1][2].

The country is also a link in the “Middle Corridor” that connects Central Asia to Europe without crossing Russia: on the same day, the foreign ministers of five Central Asian countries were in Batumi to talk about transport and transit towards the Black Sea [3][4]. A country that wants to attract these routes and investments is closely watched by its partners.
No direct effect on you in the short term. But the decision will weigh on relations between Georgia and the European Union, and so on the trade routes that cross the Caucasus.

news.2026-10-25-albanie-flamants-roses-l: Albania: five months of protests to save a lagoon and its flamingos
Since 23 May, Albanians have been protesting against a mega tourism project near the Narta lagoon. On 24 October, police again clashed with protesters in Tirana.
The movement, nicknamed the “Flamingo Revolution”, began on 23 May in the village of Zvërnec, near the Narta lagoon, against luxury resort projects linked to American investor Jared Kushner [2][3].
The largest demonstration, on 20 June, reportedly gathered more than 250,000 people according to Albanian media [3].
On 24 October, police used water cannon and tear gas against protesters demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama [1].
Key point: a foreign investment project has become Albania’s longest street protest in recent years [1][2].

The Prime Minister presents the projects as a chance to attract investors and make the country a high-end tourist destination; his opponents see protected land handed to wealthy investors without real public debate. The area is home to threatened species such as the monk seal and more than 200 bird species, and Albania’s anti-corruption body (SPAK) is investigating the land sale contracts [2][3].
If you are heading to the Albanian coast on holiday, the Vlora region is directly affected by these luxury tourism projects.

news.2026-10-25-somalie-inondations-8740: Somalia: up to 874,000 people could flee floods, and aid is lacking
The UN migration agency fears that nearly 874,000 Somalis could be displaced by the end of the year, mostly by El Niño-linked floods. It has raised only 14% of the funds it needs.
IOM and the Danish Refugee Council estimate that 874,319 people could be displaced between October and December, 92% of them because of floods [1].
The most threatened areas are Beledweyne, with nearly 229,000 people at risk, and Galkayo, with about 82,000 [1][2].
IOM has obtained only 14% of the $16.62 million it needs to prepare for El Niño-linked floods; its head in Somalia warns that the window to reduce the impact is closing [1].
Key point: we know where the water will strike, but the money to prepare is not there [1].
A flood that drives families from their fields and towns also destroys crops, livestock and roads. That pushes food prices up and makes more people depend on aid.
No direct effect on you. But climate shocks in East Africa weigh on food prices and on migration in the region.

news.2026-10-25-thailande-cambodge-front: Thailand and Cambodia: a UN-backed process tries to draw their sea border
In The Hague, the two countries agreed to stop accusing each other in public during mediation on their maritime border. The third meeting is planned for 24–27 November in Kuala Lumpur.

Cambodia launched a conciliation procedure under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea in June, after Thailand cancelled a 2001 agreement on the maritime border and joint exploitation of resources in the disputed area [1].
At the second meeting, held 14–18 October in The Hague, the two countries agreed on confidence-building measures, including the right to respond to information they consider false [1].

Thailand’s foreign minister, Sihasak Phuangketkeow, wants the process to stay limited to drawing the border; the commission reminded the parties that some commitments made have not been fully honoured [1][2].
Key point: two neighbours that have had tensions chose international mediation over confrontation [1][2].
A sea border decides who can drill, fish and lay cables in the area. Until it is drawn, the seabed resources remain blocked. The next step is the November meeting in Kuala Lumpur [1][3].
No direct effect on you, but it is an example of settling a dispute without using force.

news.2026-10-25-zambie-minerais-contre-s: Zambia: Lusaka refuses to pay for health care with its minerals and negotiates separately with Washington
Zambia signed a health agreement with the United States, then separated from it the negotiation on its critical minerals, which continues.

At the signing ceremony for the health agreement, which brings $1.5 billion in US funding, Zambia’s foreign minister, Mulambo Haimbe, said the health and critical minerals texts “need to be decoupled, and this has been done” [1][2].
The minerals deal is still being negotiated; the minister gave no details [1][2].
In May, Zambia had accused Washington of tying access to its minerals to the conclusion of the health agreement, which the US ambassador at the time called false [1][3].
Key point: the copper country refuses to let its subsoil serve as a bargaining chip for health aid [1][3].

Zambia is a major copper producer, a metal essential for cables, batteries and electric motors. The United States is seeking to secure this type of resource in the face of China. This news dates from 8 October; we include it here because the negotiation remains open.
Copper goes into almost every electrical device: what is decided in Zambia can influence their price in the long run.
US funding provided by the health agreement
news.2026-10-25-bresil-second-tour-taxe-: Brazil: on runoff day, petrol carries no federal tax
Ahead of Sunday’s runoff, Lula scrapped the federal tax on petrol for 30 days. The country votes to choose between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro.
The government scrapped for 30 days, with a possible extension, the federal petrol tax of 0.89 real per litre; it also extended the ethanol exemption and increased its subsidies [1][2].
Diesel importers receive an extra 1.40 real per litre for 30 days [1][3]. The presidency says the cost will be offset by “extraordinary revenues” from oil exports [1].
Fuel prices have climbed since the war with Iran began in late February [1]. Flávio Bolsonaro accuses Lula of “irresponsibility” and warns that diesel could rise after the election [1].
Key point: an oil-producing country is using its oil revenues to lower pump prices just before voting [1].
When oil rises, governments are tempted to cut taxes to protect purchasing power. It costs the state a lot, and prices can climb back when the measure ends.
Brazil is a major supplier of soy, coffee and oil: the election will influence the prices of what you buy.
federal tax per litre of petrol scrapped for 30 days

news.2026-10-25-petrole-116-dollars-horm: Oil at $116: Washington says the Gulf exports more than before the war, ship tracking says the opposite
Brent crude closed on Friday at around $116.7 a barrel. The US Treasury says Gulf exports exceed their pre-war level, but a ship-tracking site counts four crossings in one day at Hormuz.
Brent ended Friday at around $116.7 to $116.9, up about 3%; since the start of the year it has gained about 80% [2][3][1].

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says Gulf oil exports have exceeded their pre-war level, around 17 to 18 million barrels a day, counting the routes through Hormuz, the Gulf of Oman and the Red Sea [3]. On 20 October, Energy Secretary Chris Wright spoke of about 80% of the pre-war level [1].

A tracking site counted only 4 commercial ship crossings at Hormuz on 18 October, against about 85 a day before the crisis; the Revolutionary Guards say two supertankers hit mines, with no independent confirmation [2].
Key point: official figures and ship counts do not tell the same story, and the oil price remains very high [2][3].

At least 18 ships were attacked in two weeks according to the firm Kpler, which keeps a risk premium in prices [1]. The US government’s figures combine several routes, while the tracking counts only Hormuz crossings: both can be true at once, but they are not comparable.
Expensive oil pushes up the price of petrol, diesel and, over time, many products carried by truck or ship.

news.2026-10-25-inde-jio-record-introduc: India: Jio’s stock market debut breaks the country’s record
Jio Platforms, billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s telecoms giant, is raising 30,213 crore rupees, the biggest stock market flotation in India’s history. Its listing is expected on 28 October.
The 30,213 crore rupee offering beats the previous record, Hyundai Motor India’s in 2024 with 27,800 crore; the price range is 1,065 to 1,119 rupees a share [1].
According to AFP, the first 197.5 million shares were requested within 100 minutes; Bloomberg, cited by Börsen-Zeitung, reports bids exceeding $20 billion [2][3].
Share allotment is expected on 26 October and the stock market listing on 28 October, both indicative dates [1][3].
Key point: India now has a market able to absorb the biggest flotation in its history, despite doubts about the valuation [1][2].

An initial public offering lets a company sell shares to the public to fund its growth. Its success serves as a test of investors’ appetite for India, while expensive oil weighs on many emerging countries [2].
No direct effect on you, unless you hold funds that invest in India; but it is a signal about investor confidence in emerging countries.
